performers: Soojin Han, violin; Hankyung Arte Philharmonic; Seokwon Hong, conductor
intro: The finale of Mendelssohn’s Violin Concerto in E minor, Op. 64, begins with a short Allegretto non troppo link in E minor; the Allegro molto vivace, in E major, has trumpet calls and fast violin passagework that continues up to the closing chords. Soojin Han plays with the Hankyung Arte Philharmonic.

sections.label: Link · Solo violin and strings, E minor
sections.mNote: Allegretto non troppo: fourteen bars before the Allegro molto vivace.

sections.label: Link · Strings hold B
sections.mNote: A crescendo and diminuendo, then a held pause.

sections.label: A · Trumpet calls, violin theme, E major
sections.mNote: Allegro molto vivace opens the finale in E major.

sections.label: B · Violin theme in B major
sections.mNote: The solo melody continues in rising and falling arpeggios.

sections.label: Dev · Tune moves towards G major
sections.mNote: The orchestra’s version leads into a short development.

sections.label: A′ · Violin theme returns with strings
sections.mNote: The strings add a second melody around the soloist.

sections.label: B′ · Second theme returns, E major
sections.mNote: The short violin melody stays in the home key.

sections.label: Coda · Scales and final chords, E major
sections.mNote: Solo violin and orchestra end together in E major.

cues.title: Bridge from the Andante
cues.text: The solo violin and strings play a short bridge out of the Andante, fourteen bars in E minor marked Allegretto non troppo. The winds and brass rest while the violin plays one more phrase.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score, Rietz edition, plate M.B. 18, p. 37, Allegretto non troppo. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/a/af/IMSLP24558-PMLP04931-Mendelssohn_Violin_Concerto_Op.64.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Opening fanfares and solo entry
cues.text: Two short fanfares for bassoons, horns, trumpets and timpani open the Allegro molto vivace. Between them the violin plays a rising figure. The strings then accompany its quick tune in E major, playing lightly.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score, Rietz edition, pp. 37–38: opening fanfares, solo entry and light string accompaniment.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Finale as “fairy music”
cues.text: Steven Ledbetter described this finale as one of those brilliantly light and fleet-footed examples of “fairy music” that Mendelssohn made so uniquely his own. The strings play with light bows beneath the solo violin’s fast notes.
cues.evidence: Steven Ledbetter, Boston Symphony Orchestra programme note, on the finale as “fairy music”: https://www.bso.org/works/mendelssohn-violin-concerto Breitkopf & Härtel full score, Rietz edition, pp. 38–41, for the light string accompaniment under the solo violin: https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/a/af/IMSLP24558-PMLP04931-Mendelssohn_Violin_Concerto_Op.64.pdf

cues.title: Second theme in B major
cues.text: The solo violin plays a short, light second theme in B major. Arpeggios follow, rising and falling across the strings. The orchestra plays short phrases between the soloist’s passages.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score, Rietz edition, pp. 40–42. The B-major second theme and following arpeggios are described at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Violin_Concerto_(Mendelssohn).
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Development in G major
cues.text: The orchestra plays its own version of the opening tune, and the development moves towards G major. The violin continues in quick notes while short wind phrases enter around it.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score, Rietz edition, pp. 42–45. The orchestral variation and G-major development are described at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Violin_Concerto_(Mendelssohn).
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Return of the theme with countermelody
cues.text: The opening theme returns in the solo violin, and the strings add a new countermelody beneath it. Mendelssohn marks the passage sempre pp, always pianissimo.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score, Rietz edition, pp. 46–48: solo theme, string countermelody and sempre pp. The added countermelody is also described at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Violin_Concerto_(Mendelssohn).
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Gewandhaus concert, 23 October 1845
cues.text: On 23 October 1845 Mendelssohn conducted the Gewandhaus’s third concert of the season, and Ferdinand David played the concerto there for the second time. Mendelssohn had conducted none of the previous winter’s concerts, including the première. Over several years David had helped shape the solo part through letters and advice.
cues.evidence: Alfred Dörffel, Geschichte der Gewandhausconcerte zu Leipzig (1884), p. 111: Mendelssohn conducted part of the 1845–46 concerts and led Schumann’s B♭ symphony in the third concert, on 23 October; the same evening David played Mendelssohn’s violin concerto “zum zweiten Male”. Pp. 109–110: Mendelssohn conducted none of the 1844–45 concerts (Internet Archive, geschichtederge00konzgoog). Steven Ledbetter describes David’s advice and correspondence: https://www.bso.org/works/mendelssohn-violin-concerto

cues.title: Solo trills under the woodwinds
cues.text: The violin holds long trills while the woodwinds play the main tune. Pizzicato strings mark the pulse underneath.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score, Rietz edition, p. 52: sustained solo trills, woodwind melody and pizzicato strings.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Coda in E major
cues.text: After the trills the violin returns to running notes, and the coda moves towards E major. The orchestra plays sharply accented chords against the violin’s scales. A final upward run leads soloist and orchestra into the closing chords together.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score, Rietz edition, pp. 53–55: final solo runs, orchestral accents and E-major close.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: Dominant pedal on B before the finale
transitions.from: Link · Solo violin and strings, E minor
transitions.how: The E minor link is scored for solo violin and strings alone, with a crescendo. Its bass settles on B, the dominant of E, and the strings diminish to pianissimo. The solo violin holds above the bass, and a fermata stands over the last chord.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score, Rietz edition, p. 37, final bars of the Allegretto non troppo.

transitions.title: Fanfare after the fermata
transitions.to: A · Trumpet calls, violin theme, E major
transitions.how: After the fermata, bassoons, horns, trumpets and timpani play a fanfare at fortissimo. The marking changes to Allegro molto vivace. The solo violin follows with a rising figure, and the strings enter as the E major main theme begins.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score, Rietz edition, pp. 37–38: held dominant, fanfares and beginning of the fast solo theme.

transitions.title: Rising runs into the B major theme
transitions.from: A · Trumpet calls, violin theme, E major
transitions.to: B · Violin theme in B major
transitions.how: The violin’s rising runs and an orchestral chord lead into B major, the dominant key. The soloist begins a quieter phrase, marked leggiero, over short string chords and plucked basses. Woodwinds play in the gaps between its quick notes.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score, Rietz edition, pp. 40–41: ascent into the B-major second theme, leggiero marking and accompaniment.

transitions.title: Orchestral tutti and turn to G major
transitions.from: B · Violin theme in B major
transitions.to: Dev · Tune moves towards G major
transitions.how: The solo violin ends its B major arpeggios with a further rising scale. The orchestra then plays the opening tune fortissimo. When the violin re-enters, the harmony moves towards G major for a short development, and the strings play light chords under the solo runs.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score, Rietz edition, pp. 42–44. The G-major development after the orchestral variation is described at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Violin_Concerto_(Mendelssohn).

transitions.title: Solo return with string countermelody
transitions.from: Dev · Tune moves towards G major
transitions.to: A′ · Violin theme returns with strings
transitions.how: The solo runs lead back to the opening tune. Under the violin, the strings add a second melody, marked sempre pp, with plucked bass notes beneath. The return moves towards E major, and the woodwinds continue their short replies.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score, Rietz edition, pp. 46–48: solo return and string countermelody. The recapitulation’s added melody is described at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Violin_Concerto_(Mendelssohn).

transitions.title: The second tune returns in E
transitions.from: A′ · Violin theme returns with strings
transitions.to: B′ · Second theme returns, E major
transitions.how: The short violin tune first heard in B major returns in E major. The strings keep their clipped accompaniment and the basses punctuate the phrases. The violin soon resumes its rising and falling arpeggios, with woodwind phrases above.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score, Rietz edition, pp. 50–52. The return of the second theme in E major is described at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Violin_Concerto_(Mendelssohn).

transitions.title: Trill, scales and the E major close
transitions.from: B′ · Second theme returns, E major
transitions.to: Coda · Scales and final chords, E major
transitions.how: The strings play pizzicato while the woodwind have the tune, and the violin holds a long trill under it. The trill is followed by descending scales and then to repeated notes as the orchestra builds up. In the final stretch in E major, running figures in the violin alternate with accented chords in the orchestra. The movement ends with an upward scale.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score, Rietz edition, pp. 52–55: trills, renewed solo passagework and the E-major ending.

source.title: Mendelssohn, Violin Concerto in E minor, Op. 64, full score (Leipzig: Breitkopf & Härtel; Rietz edition, Serie 4 No. 18)
source.locator: III. Allegretto non troppo — Allegro molto vivace, pp. 37–55: string link and fanfares, p. 37; orchestral theme and development, pp. 42–45; solo trills with woodwinds, p. 52; closing pages, pp. 53–55.

timeline.note: The soloist and strings play the fourteen-bar E-minor link; winds, brass and timpani are silent.
Bassoons, horns, trumpets and timpani play two short fanfares, answered by the solo violin.
The violin’s quick E-major theme runs above a light string accompaniment.
The orchestra plays its own version of the opening tune, then the soloist rejoins for the development.
Woodwinds play the main tune again above the violin’s long trills and plucked strings.
The violin plays its last scales and the full orchestra ends in E major.

composer.epithet: Composer who wrote a work for eight string players at the age of sixteen.
facts: Ludwig Berger, piano; Carl Friedrich Zelter, composition
Düsseldorf music director, 1833–35; Leipzig Gewandhaus conductor from 1835
Married Cécile Jeanrenaud in 1837; five children; brother of Fanny Hensel
Leipzig Conservatoire, founded 1843; ten visits to Britain
composer.background:
In 1825 the sixteen-year-old Felix Mendelssohn wrote a birthday present for his violin teacher, Eduard Rietz. It was scored for four violins, two violas and two cellos, and gave Rietz a first-violin part that rises above the other seven players in long arcs. Eleven years later the composer played second viola in a public performance of the E♭ major Octet. Writing to Karl Klingemann on 31 January 1836, he admitted to “heart palpitations”.

Felix Mendelssohn was born in Hamburg on 3 February 1809; the family moved to Berlin two years later. In 1812 his sister Fanny wrote to friends in Hamburg: “Felix has a strong voice and sings all day.” His father Abraham was a banker, his grandfather Moses the Jewish philosopher. Abraham and Lea Mendelssohn had their children baptised as Christians in 1816 and used the additional surname Bartholdy. Fanny and Felix learnt piano with Ludwig Berger and composition with Carl Friedrich Zelter.
